11. Line 409-410: more elaborate explanation of why authors chose to focus on IFN-γ is
needed. They refer to a paper, but a short explanation of why this is the most interesting

Reply: Since its initial description as a soluble macromolecule “interfering” with viral
replication (PMID: 17533668), IFNγ has been extensively characterized as a pleiotropic
cytokine that modulates both innate and adaptive antiviral immune responses and can
also directly inhibit virus replication (as reviewed for instance in PMID: 30402328). In
previous studies from our group, IFNg has consistentely been the best read-out of gd T
cell reactivity against CMV-infected cells (PMID:22180442; PMID: 3262235; PMID:
34725108) and we have shown that the ability of activated gd T cell supernatants to
control virus replication is mediated by IFNγ (PMID: 22180442). These clarifications have
been added to the Results section ‘DOT cells display anti-CMV eSector functions’.

eSicient than for fibroblasts, when the CMV strain used is propagated in fibroblasts as
performed in our study (see for instance PMID: 2550582). The low percentage of infected
endothelial cells shown in Figure S4A of the revised manuscript was therefore expected.
As a consequence, the reactivity of DOT cells is expected to be less important against
infected endothelial cells compared to infected fibroblasts, as shown in Figure S4D of
the revised manuscript. When IL-18 is added to co-cultures (Fig. 2B), it potentiates CMV-
induced IFNg production (as described in Guerville et al., Oncoimmunol 2015; PMID:
26155394). In cocultures with endothelial cells, IL-18 therefore reveals a reactivity
otherwise invisible.

16. Figure 2D: please explain the use of HSV and VZV in more detail. Why are they used
as controls? Are there controls used to show successful infection, what is their
infection rate? Infection and expression of specific antigen (IE-1) is shown for CMV-
infected cells, but not for HSV and VZV-infected cells. Is this the correct infection model
these viruses? A bit of background is needed. And also are these still considered the
right controls considering that later in the paper is shown that the cells do not require
TCR engagement.
Reply: HSV and VZV are used as controls because they belong to the same family of
Herpesviridae as CMV and share genetic similarities (PMID: 2552898). They also can be
easily compared to CMV in vitro since they can readily infect fibroblasts, which are the
prototypic target cells used for in vitro infection by the three viruses. We have already
shown in previously published studies (Halary et al., JEM 2005 PMID: 15897274; Kaminski
et al., JID 2021 PMID: 32622351) that HSV-1 and VZV-infected fibroblasts do not activate
Vd2neg gd T cells. This is consistant with the absence of gd T cell responses in kidney
transplant recipients infected with HSV or VZV, by contrats to patients infected with CMV
(Dechanet et al., JID 1999 PMID: 9841815; Kaminski et al., JID 2021 PMID: 32622351). In
vitro, successful infection can be determined by observing the cytopathic eSects of these
3 lytic viruses by microscopy. We then used cultures with the same rates of cytopathic
eSect (in between 50% and 100%) to compare DOT cell reactivities.
Interestingly, and as mentioned by the reviewer, even though the activation of DOT cells
by CMV-infected cells is TCR-independent, it remains specific of CMV when compared
to VZV and HSV, indicating that the induction of other molecules than a TCRligand can be
specific of one virus. Alternatively, VZV and HSV could encode unique immune evasion
mechanisms absent during CMV infection.

33. Figure 5G: 2 doses of cells given à how does this compare to the dosing regimen in

Reply: Although a γδ T cell therapy has not yet been tested in humans to treat CMV
infection, we can compare the numbers of mouse γδ T cells administered in our in vivo
experiments (Figure 4 of the revised manuscript) to the numbers of infused CMV-specific
CD8⁺ T cells in Smith et al. (Clin Infect Dis 2019 DOI: 10.1093/cid/ciy549) and Khoury et
al. (Am J Transplant 2024, DOI: 10.1016/j.ajt.2024.04.009). These two pioneering studies
evaluated CMV-specific CD8⁺ T cell adoptive transfer to treat CMV infection in solid-
organ transplant recipients.
In Khoury et al., patients received a median of two infusions of virus-specific T cells at a
dose of 50 × 10⁶/m² body surface area. In Smith et al., patients received up to six doses
of in vitro-expanded T cells at 10–20 × 106/m² every two weeks.
In our experiments, Rag−/−γc−/− mice received 10⁶ γδ T cells on day 0 and day 7. Given
their average body surface area of 0.007 m², this equates to 143 × 10⁶/m² per dose. This
means the mice received approximately three times the maximal dose used in Khoury et
al., and 2.4 times the maximal dose used in Smith et al. Thus, the γδ T cell dose
administered to the mice falls within the range of those used in these two human trials.
We have also modified the labels and legends in Fig. 4G of the revised manuscript
(previously Fig. 5G) to improve clarity.

diSerence between MCMV status of donor mice (P = 0.0837).

compared to those that succumbed) but does not allow to draw a causative conclusion.
In the revised manuscript this figure is now positionned as Fig. S7A.
To formally test whether γδ T cell adoptive transfer can control MCMV viral load in
infected mice, we performed an additional experiment using the same protocol as in the
previous Fig. 5I. MCMV-infected Rag-/-γc-/- mice were adoptively transferred with γδ T
cells amplified from MCMVpos (n=5) or MCMVneg (n=5) C57BL/6J donor mice, or with
RPMI as a control (n=5). All mice were sacrificed at day 14 post MCMV infection to allow
direct comparison of viral loads. This experiment showed that the transfer of γδ T cells
amplified from both MCMVpos and MCMVneg donor mice significantly reduced viral
loads in the spleen, liver, and lungs compared to RPMI-treated controls, demonstrating
that γδ T cell adoptive transfer induces a decrease in viral load. This new experiment is
now included in the revised manuscript as Figure 4J.
36. Figure 5J: Please comment on what the ‘eSector memory population’ would be. In
the text it is said the transferred T cells had a ‘TEM phenotype’ (line 521-522) but TEM is
characterized as CD62L-, CD44- in the figure legend. The majority of cells is CD62L-
,CD44+.
Reply: Thank you for this valuable comment. There was an error in the legend of this
figure: TEM cells are CD62L⁻ CD44⁺, not CD44⁻. We have corrected the legend of Figure
4E (previously Figure 5E) accordingly.
37. Line 524-525: this is a strong conclusion which is not entirely supported by the
presented data mainly in figure 5H and I. In addition, it should be discussed whether
this is the right mouse model to makes these conclusions.
Reply: Please refer to our responses to comments 34 and 35, where new experiments
have been carried out to support these conclusions. We have also revised our conclusion
as follows: “Together, these findings demonstrate that adoptively transferred γδ T cells
can migrate to MCMV-infected organs, control viral replication, and protect
immunodeficient mice from lethal MCMV infection”.
The main advantage of this mouse model of MCMV infection is its similarity to human
CMV pathogenesis. It induces a systemic disease, as observed in humans, and is widely
used, making it an appropriate model for testing new cell therapies. However, its primary
limitation is that it does not allow testing of human DOT cells. Nevertheless, we
addressed this limitation by generating murine “DOT-like” cells that exhibit the same
central memory phenotype as human DOT cells and shared their anti-CMV activity. In the
future, humanized CMV mouse models could provide additional insight into the eSicacy
of human DOT cells in vivo.
These additional points have been incorporated into the discussion section of the revised
manuscript.
38. Title of last results paragraph (p24): we do not agree that the DOT cells ‘meet cell
therapy requirements’. This is a generalization. While the DOT cells may meet some
requirements, the data presented does not unequivocally show it meets all the cell
therapy requirements.
Reply: This is a fair comment. To take it into account, we have split the final section of
the Results into two parts with more appropriate titles.
- The first paragraph, which includes Table 1 and Fig. 5A-D, is now titled “Autologous
CMV-reactive DOT cells can be obtained from SOTR”.
- The second paragraph, which includes Fig. 5E-I and Fig. S8, is now titled “DOT cells
remain functional under immunosuppression”.
39. Line 544: please explain why it is necessary to add IL-15 to these cultures. Is IL-15
needed to make the cells less vulnerable for the immune suppressive drugs? And how
does this relate to the in vivo situation?
Reply: IL-15 is essential to support the survival of DOT cells both in vitro and in vivo (in
NSG mice), as demonstrated in previous studies (Mensurado et al., Blood 2024 PMID:
38437507; Blanco-Dominguez et al., Nat Cancer 2025 PMID: 40240620). Following
expansion, DOT cells are systematically rested in complete medium supplemented with
IL-15 prior to their use in functional assays, including the proliferation and reactivity
assays in the presence of immunosuppressive drugs shown in Figure 5 of the revised
manuscript (described in the Methods section).
Regarding the in vivo relevance, several studies have shown that IL-15 levels increase
during CMV infection. For instance, increased IL-15 mRNA levels have been observed in
the bone marrow of CMV-seropositive individuals compared to CMV-seronegative
individuals (Pangrazzi et al., Front Immunol 2017, PMID: 28674537). Additionally, ICU
patients exhibit higher levels of IL-15 before CMV reactivation, compared to controls
(Chiche et al., Crit Care Med 2012, PMID: 22971588). Based on this evidence, we can
speculate that the production of IL-15 during CMV infection may similarly support DOT
cell survival in vivo.
40. Figure 6F and H: please comment on the very low proliferation index observed (high
contrast with the DOT expansion protocol from healthy donors) and the relatively low
amounts of live cells? H also doesn’t have statistics.
Reply: The aim of this experiment was to evaluate the survival and proliferation of DOT
cells in vitro, in the presence of immunosuppressive drugs. For this, we measured their
proliferation capacity and viability in culture during 15 days, after the end of their
amplification. Once amplified, their proliferation index was expected to be lower than
during their amplification phase.
The number of living cells did not exceed 50% at the end of the culture, indicating a
certain degree of cell death. Nevertheless, their proliferation capacity still allowed for the
renewal of a suSicient number of DOT cells to maintain the DOT cell population at day 15
at the same level as on day 0 (see Fig. 5G of the revised manuscript).
Furthermore, we would like to highlight that for the experiments presented in panels E-
F-G-H-I, we used DOT cells amplified from healthy donors.
In summary, their ability to persist for 15 days in vitro suggests that DOT cells could
survive in vivo for days or weeks after infusion. This was confirmed in our mouse model,
where in vitro amplified gd T cells cells were found in infected organs more than 15 days
after infusion.
Fig. 5H now shows P values (determined by repeated-measures one-way ANOVA).
41. Figure 6I: what is the dotted line representing? Mock+DOT as a baseline? Please
explain?
Reply: The dotted line indeed represented Mock+DOT at baseline but did not provide any
relevant additional information to interprete this figure. As a result, we have removed the
dotted line to avoid any confusion in the interpretation of the figure.
42. Figure legend for 6 on p. 44. Inconsistent representation of ‘donors’ vs.
‘experiments’. Sometimes donors are mentioned, sometimes it’s ‘representative
experiments’ but are these then from same donor? Please make this consistent and
clear how many donors (patients or healthy) are used per experiment.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We have now clarified the number of
donors used in each panel of the figure. Specifically, for panels A to D, DOT cells were
amplified from 8 kidney transplant recipients. For panels E to I, DOT cells were amplified
from healthy donors. 4 donors were used for panels E and F, 3 donors for panels G and H,
and 5 donors for panel I.
In the revised manuscript, Figure 6 has been renumbered as Figure 5.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
1. The authors present interesting data regarding an adoptive gamma-delta T cell based
approach using only 50 ml of patient blood to tackle CMV disease which are of
significance to the field, however to increase rigor, the amount of donors should be
increased to show be more convincing.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. In response, we have increased
the number of donors analyzed to strengthen the robustness of our findings. Specifically:
- Fig. 1E: this analysis is now performed on DOT cells from n=6 donors (three
CMVneg and three CMVpos) instead of n=4 previously.
- Fig. 3B: this analysis is now performed on DOT cells from n=8 donors (previously
n=4).
- Fig. 3C and 3D: gdTCR knockout experiments were performed on an additional
DOT donor, for a total of n=3.
- Fig. 3E: we now present an analysis on n=6 donors, instead of one representative
donor shown previously.
- Fig. 3H: ICAM1 and LFA1 blocking experiments were performed on three
additional DOT donors, for a total of n=6.
- Fig. 5A-D: DOT cells were amplified from three additional kidney transplant
recipients, for a total of n=8. In Fig. 5D, all 8 patients are now represented in the
same graph (each datapoint corresponds to the mean of culture triplicates for one
patient).
Across the revised manuscript, each analysis is now based on a minimum of n=3 healthy
donors or patients. Technical replicates are no longer represented in figure panels, with
the exception of Fig. 3D and Fig. S5 (gdTCR knockout experiments), where each donor is
shown on an individual graph.
2. I would recommend the following adjustments:
- l. 370: The numbers/percentages of TEMRA should be mentioned.
Reply: We have now included the relevant percentages in the revised Results section:
- In CMV-seronegative donors, naïve cells represented 74.0 ± 18.8% of Vd2neg gd T
cells at day 0.
- In CMV-seropositive donors, TEMRA cells represented 41.2 ± 19.8% of Vd2neg gd T
cells at day 0.
- At day 21, DOT cells from both CMV-seronegative and CMV-seropositive donors
were predominantly central memory cells (88.1 ± 9.2% and 88.1 ± 9.6% of
Vd2neg gd T cells respectively).
3. - At least 6 donors should be shown for each experiment, preferentially 3 females and
3 males, technical replicates are less relevant, they can be used to calculate a
medium/median for each donor
Reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to strengthen the robustness of our study
by increasing donor numbers and considering sex balance.
While we were not able to include six donors for every experiment, we have increased
donor numbers throughout the manuscript wherever possible (as detailed in our
response to comment 1). All analyses are now performed on a minimum of three
independent donors, and all analyses presented in Figure 1 and 2 were performed on a
minimum of 6 donors. Regarding donor sex, we regret that we do not have access to this
information for the healthy donor samples used in this study. Regarding kidney transplant
recipients, the sex of the patients is now included in Table 1 of the revised manuscript.
We agree with the reviewer that technical replicates are less informative than biological
replicates, and we have revised the presentation of our data accordingly: individual data
points now represent means for each donor, and technical replicates are no longer
shown in the figures (except in Fig. 3D and Fig. S5, where each donor is presented
separately).
We hope that this expanded dataset addresses the reviewer’s concerns, as it enhances
the robustness of our findings.
4. The appropriateness of the mouse experiment should be further discussed regarding
diSerences of humans and mice gamma-delta T cells.
Reply: The main advantage of this mouse model of MCMV infection is its similarity to
human CMV pathogenesis. It induces a systemic disease, as observed in humans, and is
widely used, making it an appropriate model for testing new cell therapies. Furthermore
we have previously shown that MCMV induces long-term expansion of murine γδ T cells
that protect mice from the infection, very similarly to what can be observed in human
CMV infection (PMID: 25747674 ; PMID: 38976755). MCMV is then precisely an
interesting model to make parallels between human and mouse γδ T cells. However, the
primary limitation of this MCMV model is that it does not allow testing of human DOT
cells. Nevertheless, we addressed this limitation by generating murine “DOT-like” cells
that exhibited the same central memory phenotype as human DOT cells and shared their
anti-CMV activity. In the future, humanized CMV mouse models could provide additional
insight into the eSicacy of human DOT cells in vivo. We have incorporated these
comments into the discussion section.
5. l. 501: All data should be shown either in the supplement or main figures, not showing
data is not acceptable.
Reply: We agree with the reviewer that all data described in the manuscript should be
shown. In order to simplify the lecture for the reader, we have deleted this sentence
from the manuscript.
6. l. 528: Is there supporting evidence for this claim, especially having in mind the
TRACE study?
Reply: Both autologous and allogeneic virus-specific cell therapies have been or are
currently being tested in phase I trials in SOTR (PMID: 29982441; PMID: 38643944;
ACTRN12621000323820) or following allogeneic stem cell transplantation (TRACE study,
NCT04832607). We agree that there is currently no direct evidence that “an allogeneic T-
cell therapy would eventually be rejected by the host immune system, thus limiting its
long-term eSicacy”. This was merely a hypothesis, and we have removed this sentence.
7. l.532: Actually, there are many reports showing successful expansion of autologous T
cell products from kidney transplanted patients, please show evidence or adjust the
statement (e.g. 10.3389/fimmu.2019.01148).
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this fair comment, but there is currently no data showing
successful expansion of autologous gd T cells from solid organ transplant recipients
receiving immunosupressants. To address this comment, we have adjusted the
introduction of this paragraph and added references regarding the successful expansion
of autologous ab T cell products from solid organ transplant recipients as follows:
“Both autologous and allogeneic virus-specific T cell therapies have been or are currently
being tested in phase I trials in SOTR15,17,42 (CTRN12621000323820) or in a phase III trial
in HSCTR (TRACE study: NCT04832607). Among these two strategies, the autologous
approach is particularly attractive in SOTR to avoid the risk of allosensitization
deleterious to the transplant43. However, whether functional and CMV-reactive DOT cells
can be amplified from immunosuppressed transplant recipients remains to be
evaluated.”
8. l. 542: What was the rationale to exclude glucocorticoids from the study, although
they are standard immunosuppressants used after SOT? Please add data on the eSect
of glucocorticoids on the cell product.
Reply: As requested, we have tested the impact of glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone)
on DOT cell proliferation and anti-CMV reactivity in vitro. At the concentrations used in
the maintenance treatment of SOTR (at around 10 ng/ml 12 hours after the ingestion)
(PMID: 9797792), methylprednisolone did not inhibit the persistence and reactivity of
DOT cells against CMV-infected fibroblasts. These new data are now presented in
Supplementary Figure 8 of the revised manuscript.
9. Please add data on the killing capacity of patient derived T cell products regarding
killing of the CMV+ fibroblasts.
Reply: Demonstrating the killing capacity of DOT cells against CMV-infected fibroblasts
is technically challenging. Indeed, CMV infection is lytic and eventually leads to
fibroblast death independently of T cell cytotoxicity. 5 days of infection, when DOT cells
are cocultured with fibroblasts, is the limit to keep infected cells reasonably alive, making
it technically unfeasible to distinguish additional killing mediated by DOT cells. Moreover,
killing infected cells is not necessarily the most important function of gd T cells in the
context of CMV infection. Secreting IFNg, which has potent anti-viral functions and
inhibits CMV replication is also critical to control the virus propagation.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The paper by Marsères et al. asks whether the long-established capacity of human non-
Vδ2+ T cells to respond to CMV-infected cells (and, at the same time, tumor cells) can
be exploited as a cell therapy using the DOT cell technique to propagate and enrich for
Vδ1+ T cells. Overall, the results seem encouraging and provide a basis for considering
a clinical trial to limit CMV infection or reactivation in immunosuppressed transplant
recipients. This is a major unmet need although analogous clinical approaches using αβ
T cells are further advanced. For the most part, the experiments are logical and seem
well-executed, but there are areas where the authors’ interpretations need to be placed
very clearly in the context of DOT cells since they may not apply to human γδ T cells in
vivo. Indeed, this is an immunotherapy paper rather than a paper about human
immunology, which is fine, so long as the two are not confused.
Main points:
1. Figure 1: this shows that DOT cells can be expanded equally well from CMV-sero(+)
donor and CMV-sero(-) donors, thereby showing that an initial status of terminally
diSerentiated eSector non-Vd2+ cells in CMV-sero(+) donors does not prevent the cells
expanding and adopting a phenotype more like activated central memory cells.
However, a major advantage of γδ T cells for immunotherapy is their lack of MHC
restriction and potential to be used in the allogeneic setting, in which case, a set of
CMV-sero(-) donors would presumably be the main source. Hence, why is it important
to know that cells from CMV-sero(+) donors can be expanded? The authors might argue
that this is because autologous cells may be required for solid-organ recipients, but for
that setting, which is a major unmet need, the authors need to be much more clear
about the advantages over autologous αβ T cells.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this comment. As correctly pointed out, the relevance
of expanding DOT cells from CMV-seropositive donors depends on the therapeutic
setting (allogeneic or autologous). At this stage, both allogeneic and autologous DOT cell
therapies can be considered.
In the allogeneic setting, access to a broad and diverse donor pool is essential. CMV
prevalence exceeds 50% in most western countries, reaching for instance over 70% in
Spain and Portugal (PMID: 38275940). Demonstrating that DOT cells can be eSiciently
expanded from CMV-seropositive donors ensures broad donor availability, making it
feasible to manufacture a diverse and partially HLA-matched donor bank. This could
reduce the risk of allosensitization and more specifically the occurrence of donor-
specific antibodies in transplant recipients.
In the autologous setting, refractory CMV infections typically occur in CMV-seronegative
patients (transplanted with an organ coming from a CMV-seropositive donor) whose
adaptive immune response to CMV is lacking (PMID: 26054538). In this context,
generating DOT cells from the γδ T cell pool of these patients may oSer an advantage:
naïve γδ T cells can be expanded ex vivo into functional and CMV-reactive DOT cells,
whereas it is challenging to obtain CMV-specific memory αβ T cells from naïve cells
(PMID: 25925682).
These points are now included in the Discussion section of the revised manuscript.
2. Figure 2: this shows that DOT cells from sero(+) or sero(-) donors limit CMV
dissemination in vitro. However, the data do not seem as simple as the text describes.
First, there is rather marginal activation of cytolysis by CMV-infected fibroblasts
compared to medium alone, whereas the strong activation of cytolysis against infected
macrophages is barely greater than that against mock-infected macrophages. For
putative DOT-immunotherapy the fibroblast data might question eSicacy, whereas the
macrophage data might question safety. The IFNγ data seem more convincing.
Reply: We agree that IFNg secretion assays provide a more convincing indication of DOT
cell anti-CMV reactivity compared to CD107a assays. However, we would like to argue
that the combined eSects of IFNg secretion and the limited, yet statistically significant,
cytotoxic activity likely act synergistically to limit CMV dissemination, as illustrated in
Figure 2F.
Regarding the safety concern raised about macrophage targeting, we would like to clarify
that the macrophages used in these experiments are M1-like activated macrophages,
generated by diSerentiating monocytes in the presence of GM-CSF for six days. These
activated macrophages diSer substantially from resting tissue macrophages, which
mitigates potential safety issues raised by the reviewer. Importantly, this diSerentiation
and activation step is necessary to render macrophages permissive to CMV infection and
may explain why they induce a basal activation of DOT cells. This notwithstanding,
infection by CMV significantly further increased DOT cell degranulation and IFNg
secretion, underscoring the capacity of CMV to activate DOT cells.
3. The specificity for CMV versus other viruses is striking, but this needs to be
considered in the context of Fig 3.
Fig 3: this shows that the TCR is not required for targeting CMV-infected cells. Note, the
abstract states: “DOT cells eSiciently controlled CMV dissemination in vitro. This
antiviral eSect was independent of the γδTCR”. This seems very surprising given the
wealth of evidence from this team that the TCRs of human non-Vδ2 T cells recognise
self-antigens upregulated on CMV-infected cells. Furthermore, it was reasonable to
assume that such TCR reactivities would account for CMV-specificity (above).
Reply: This issue of human non-Vδ2 T cells specificity for CMV is undoubtly an interesting
and striking point. This specificity is observed both in patients (only CMV infection can
induce non-Vg9Vδ2 T cell response and expansion, not HSV or VZV; Déchanet et al., JID
1999; Pitard et al., Blood 2008; Kaminski et al., JID 2021) and in vitro (only CMV infection
can induce fibroblast ability to activate non-Vg9Vδ2 T cells; Halary et al., JEM 2005;
Kaminski et al., JID 2021). However, it is not clear at all whether TCR reactivities account
for CMV-specificity. We have for instance shown in one of our study (Willcox et al., Nat
Immunol 2012) that the Vg4Vd5 T cell clone LES was recognizing EPCR, a constitutively
expressed ligand on fibroblasts. The specificity of this clone for CMV-infected cells was
dependent on the strong induction of CD54/ICAM-1 expression by CMV. Hence, CMV
specificity is most probably due to its capacity to induce a multimolecular stress
signature on infected cells recognized not only by the TCR but also by co-stimulatory
molecules such as LFA-1. Why HSV-1 and VZV cannot induce the same signature is
currently not resolved, but might rely on inhibitory signals preventing gd T cell activation.
Regarding the TCR-independent CMV recognition by DOT cells, we are not as surprised
as the reviewer. All our previous studies were conducted using non-Vδ2 T cell clones, or
non-Vδ2 T cells isolated from CMV-infected transplant patients (which repertoire is highly
restricted or even oligoclonal in some patients, Dechanet et al , JCI 1999). On the
contrary, the repertoire of DOT cells has been shown to be highly polyclonal (Di Lorenzo
et al., Cancer Immunol Res 2019, PMID: 30894378) supposedly because they expand
from naïve cells. Then, it would have been more surprising to observe TCR-specificity of
a polyclonal population. Tumor cell recognition by DOT cells was also previously shown
to be TCR-independent by the team of B Silva-Santos (Di Lorenzo et al., Cancer Immunol
Res 2019).
4. So, do the data hold up? The use of a blocking antibody is problematic because
without a clear control to prove otherwise, it is common for anti-TCR antibodies, even
those that can block, to cross-link TCRs, thereby clouding the interpretation. Therefore,
the logical experiment is to delete the TCR, which is accomplished. Here the problem
may be that (according to the Methods) the TCR deletion was validated over a 4-day
period after which cells were rested overnight, and then used in the experiments. Prior
to this, the cells had constant TCR stimulation for over two weeks and probably
therefore carry a legacy of this exposure in terms of downstream signalling eSectors
and epigenetic imprinting.
Reply: We fully agree with the reviewer’s interpretation. We had attempted to address this
point in the discussion, but our explanation may not have been suSiciently clear. We did
not mean that TCR signaling is not necessary for the overall DOT cell response. Rather,
our data indicate that during the interaction with CMV-infected cells, TCR engagement is
not necessary for DOT cell activation, as evidenced by the robust response of TCR-
knockout DOT cells to CMV-infected, compared to mock-infected targets (Fig. 3D and
Fig. S5B of the revised manuscript). In other words, the specific recognition of CMV-
infected cells by DOT cells does not require ligand recognition by the TCR. We propose
that the DOT cell expansion procedure, which involves constant TCR signalling, provides
an essential initial TCR signalling (that could be considered as a priming), and that CMV-
infected cells then provide the costimulation, leading to a CMV-specific response.
To clarify this distinction in the manuscript, we have revised our wording by replacing
“TCR-independent response” by “TCR-independent recognition” or by saying that TCR-
engagement is not required during the interaction with CMV-infected cells.
5. This could explain why the evident reduction in IFNg response (Fig 3E) is not
complete. The hypothesis that TCR signalling is required could explain why there was no
impact of blocking any NKRs (Fig 3G) and seems to be supported by the data in Fig 4
(below).
Also, the argument that the high background of IFNγ in DOT cells responding to mock-transfected cells
probably relates to a legacy of continued TCR signalling does not seem consistent with there being no background IFNγ in
cells stimulated with isotype antibodies as a control for anti-CD3 (compare Fig 3D and 3E).
Reply: We respectfully disagree with this comment and would like to clarify the data as
follows:
- In Fig. S5B of the revised manuscript (previously Fig. 3E), we can see that the
background of IFNg production by control DOT cells is comparable between
“medium” alone and “mock” conditions, indicating that coculture with mock-
infected fibroblasts does not induce a consistant additional background
activation in these 3 DOT donors.
- In Fig. S5A of the revised manuscript (previously Fig. 3D), there is indeed
background IFNg secretion in the “Isotype” control condition, but because of the
scale, it is not visible on the graph. When the same data are plotted on the same
axis (as shown in Figure R5 below), it becomes visible that IFNg background levels
are in the same range in the “isotype” condition of Fig. S5A and in the “medium”
and “mock” conditions of Fig. S5B.
Figure R5: IFNg secretion by DOT cells from 3 independent donors (51, 84 and R6),
incubated for 24h in medium alone, with an isotype control antibody, or with mock-
infected fibroblasts.
This basal secretion of IFNg is consistent with the “legacy of continued TCR signaling”
argued by the reviewer and that we fully agree with. The abrogation of this IFNg production
background in TCR-KO DOT cells allows to reveal the “true” CMV-specific response, as
shown in the green histograms in Fig. S5B and Fig. 3D of the revised manuscript. Notably,
the fold increase in IFNγ production by TCR-KO DOT cells in response to CMV-infected
cells exceeded 15-fold (Fig. 3D), suggesting that the TCR-independent signals induced
by CMV-infected cells are very potent and may play a crucial role in their activity.
6. Fig 4: this claims to show that LFA1 is important for the response to CMV-infected
cells. This would be consistent with the TCR engaging CMV-infected targets and
activating LFA1 via inside-out signalling, thereby enhancing intimate eSector-target cell
contacts. One can hypothesise that in TCRk.o. cells, residual signalling events following
exposure to chronic TCR signalling are suSicient to activate LFA1. Indeed, if the TCR was
not involved, and none of the NKRs examined in Fig 3G is involved, it is very challenging
to understand how activating LFA1 alone could induce a response from T cells, since it
is at best a co-stimulator and primarily an adhesion molecule.
Reply: We show in Fig. 3F of the revised manuscript that a recombinant ICAM-1-Fc protein
or an agonist anti-LFA-1 antibody can activate DOT cells even when used alone. This
demonstrates that LFA-1 engagement, independently of TCR engagement, can activate
DOT cells. LFA-1 engagement by CMV-infected cells might therefore be suSicient to
activate TCR-KO DOT cells. It is possible that this response requires a prior activation of
the gdTCR during DOT cell expansion, that would activate LFA-1 via inside-out signalling.
We however cannot exclude the involvement of other undetermined activating
receptor(s) during the co-culture with CMV-infected cells.
7. It is perhaps important to note that if the TCR were not required, the authors would be
obliged to explain why transfer of γδ T cells would be preferable to transferring NK cells.
In fact, the response of donor 2 LFA1k.o. cells (Fig 4E) is interpreted as negative, but it
looks equally as strong as the responses of donors 1 and 2 TCRk.o. cells (Fig 3E) which
were scored as positive.
Reply: Regarding the adoptive transfer of gd T cells versus NK cells, please see our
response to comment 9 below.
It is diSicult to compare the response of DOT cells between Figure 3 and Figure 4 of the
original manuscript, because they have been generated from diSerent donors. As the
reviewer can appreciate in Fig. 2B, IFNg production is very variable from one DOT cell
product to another.
We would like to mention here our reply to Reviewer 1 comment 29:
Reply: We appreciate this important comment and fully agree that conclusions drawn
from a single donor with eSicient knockout are insuSicient. To address this comment, we
attempted LFA-1 knockout in DOT cells from three additional donors. Knockout eSiciency
was assessed by flow cytometry (Figure R4).
Unfortunately, these three attempts to obtain a full knockout failed (as shown in Figure
R4 below), as LFA-1 expression remained high following editing. We also attempted to
enrich LFA1-negative cells by cell sorting, but in all cases, we were unable to recover a
suSicient number of viable cells for downstream functional assays. Given these
technical limitations, we have decided to remove the initial LFA-1 knockout data from the
manuscript. Instead, conclusions about the involvement of LFA-1 in CMV-specific
reactivity are now based on functional experiments using anti ICAM1 and LFA-1 blocking
antibodies, now performed in six independent DOT donors in total. These results
consistently support a role for LFA-1 in DOT cell anti-CMV reactivity.
We have revised Figure 3 and Figure 4 accordingly. The two figures are now merged in
one. In the revised manuscript, we have mentioned this technical limitation in the Results
section. We have also revised our interpretation and discussion of this mechanism
accordingly (in the Discussion section).
8. In sum, it seems highly likely to this reviewer that human Vδ1 cells require the TCR to
engage CMV-infected cells and that they then activate LFA1. In DOT cells, LFA1 is
already activated by chronic TCR signalling and can collaborate with residual TCR
signals in TCR k.o. cells. This is an unusual situation that should not be confused with
human immunology.
Reply: We thank the reviewer for this summary that fits perfectly with our own
interpretation. We agree that DOT cell activity cannot be compared to the physiological
activity of non-Vd2 T cells. As pointed out by the reviewer, our previous studies have
consistently shown that non-Vd2 T cells, including Vd1 T cells, recognize CMV-infected
cells in a TCR-dependent manner (Halary et al., JEM 2005; Willcox et al., Nat Immunol
2012; Kaminski et al., JID 2021).
DOT cells represent a highly activated cell product, shaped by in vitro expansion and
chronic TCR engagement, leading to a unique way of responding to CMV-infected cells.
While this does not directly reflect the physiology of human non-Vd2 T cells, it is essential
to dissect the functional requirements of DOT cells to develop them as a therapeutic
product, which was the purpose of our study. We have clarified this point in the revised
manuscript (Results and Discussion sections).
9. Fig 5: this shows that murine γδ T cells produced via a DOT-type culture can be
transferred to recipient lymphocyte, ILC, and NK cell deficient mice, wherein they
become activated and distribute into multiple organs to limit CMV in vivo. This is a
proof-of-principle; one suspects that NK cells might have achieved the same outcome.
Reply: We agree with the reviewer that our in vivo experiments using murine γδ T cells
generated via a DOT-like protocol serve as a proof-of-principle.
NK cells indeed have well-established antiviral functions, including against CMV,
even
though the demonstrations have been mainly obtained in mice. However, there are at
least two reasons why DOT cells may oSer distinct advantages or complement NK-based
therapies:
- We have shown that the DOT protocol allows for a robust and eSicient expansion
of clinically relevant numbers of non-Vδ2 T cells from the peripheral blood of both
healthy individuals and immunosuppressed transplant recipients. In contrast,
generating large-scale, functional NK cell products can be more variable and often
requires longer culture times or feeder-cell systems, which pose regulatory and
translational challenges (PMID: 38443448; PMID: 40681797).
- DOT cell harbour a unique landscape of receptors, notably lacking expression of
NKG2A and KIRs (Fig. 1G and Figure R6 below). These receptors are classically
expressed by NK cells, contribute to their recognition of CMV-infected cells, and
are common targets of CMV-induced immune evasion strategies
(PMID: 12032324, PMID: 18069056, PMID: 29632329). Many evasion
mechanisms have been selected by CMV to escape from NK cell control, which
has not been reported yet to our knowledge for gd T cells or DOT cells. In addition,
as discussed above, TCR priming during the expansion phase most likely
participates in the overall response of DOT cells to CMV, distinguishing them from
a NK cell product. Altogether, the molecular mechanisms underlying CMV
recognition by DOT and NK cells are likely distinct.
Figure R6: NKG2A expression on DOT cells.
DOT cells amplified from three independent donors (88, 97 and 98) were stained with
antibodies directed against the populations markers CD3, gdTCR, Vd1 TCR and Vd2 TCR
and the NK receptor NKG2A. Shown are percentages of NKG2A+ Vd2neg gd T cells.
Fluorescence Minus One controls were used to set positivity gates.
Fig 6: this shows that the DOT protocol can be applied to kidney transplant recipients
and that the cells may be functional in the presence of common immunosuppressants
that would be the milieu for an adoptive therapy. This is encouraging although no
evidence is given for how the cells remain functional in the immunosuppressants.
Reply: Cyclosporin and Tacrolimus are calcineurin inhibitors that block NFAT
translocation and IL-2 production in T cells. However, the DOT protocol does not rely on
IL-2. Instead, it relies on IL-15 as the critical cytokine during the second stage of
expansion and diSerentiation (day 7 to day 21 of expansion). Moreover, IL-15 has been
shown to enhance DOT cell therapeutic eSicacy in vivo (Sanchez Martinez et al., J
Immunother Cancer 2022, PMID: 36162920; Blanco-Dominguez et al., Nat Cancer 2025,
PMID: 40240620). Importantly, IL-15 signalling is independent of the calcineurin-NFAT
pathway. Based on these observations, we hypothesize that DOT cells are more
dependent on IL-15 than IL-2 signaling and are therefore resistant to the eSects of
calcineurin inhibitors.
Regarding Everolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, we have previously shown that, at clinically
relevant concentrations such as used in a transplantation setting, everolimus does not
prevent T cell proliferation nor response to CMV, and by contrast promotes T cell survival
and prevents T cell dysfunctionality (Kaminski et al., JASN 2022, PMID: 34725108).
Consistently, Everolimus has been associated with a reduced occurrence of CMV
infections in transplant recipients in several independent studies (PMID: 34990047;
PMID: 31152476; PMID: 25988935).
We have summarized these points in the discussion section of the revised manuscript.

Point-by-point response
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Reviewer Response to Rebuttal Letter (Reviewer #1 + co-reviewer) :
We would like to begin by congratulating the authors on the work they have put into
revising their manuscript. The additional experiments, clarifications to the figures, and
improvements to the text have significantly enhanced the quality of the work. We
especially appreciate the consistency in which CMV status of the donor cells is now
shown in the figures, providing transparency in the functional equivalence of the DOT
cells expanded from diDerent donors. These thoughtful revisions demonstrate a strong
commitment to scientific rigor and communication, and we commend the authors for
their eDorts.
Reply: We thank the reviewers for their kind comments.
That said, we would like to kindly request the authors to address a few remaining points:
1. Inclusion of Reviewer-Specific Figures
Several figures created specifically in response to reviewer comments (the CRISPOR
output data with sgRNA specificity scores, and specifically R1 and R3) provide valuable
insights and clarity. We believe these should be included in the supplemental data to
ensure transparency and to benefit future readers. Figure R1 addresses baseline gating
data often requested in the field for assay validation purposes. Furthermore, figure R3
shows important data serving as a positive control for main figure 3B, without which the
main figure is not adequately interpretable.
Reply: All requested figures have now been included in the supplementary materials of
the revised manuscript. The gRNA characterization table (previously Figure R3) was
included as Supplementary Table 2. Figure R1 (Fluorescence Minus One controls from
the diDerent culture conditions) was included as Supplementary Figure 4b. Finally,
Figure R3 (positive control experiment for Vd1 TCR blocking) was included as
Supplementary Figure 5a.
2. Clarification on Specific Findings
We would appreciate further commentary on the following points:
• Comment #14 and #39: While the authors have touched on the presence of IL-18 (in
CMV-infected human endothelial cells) and IL-15 (in bone marrow of CMV-infected
individuals), a more detailed contextualization would strengthen the author’s views on
what this means regarding the survival and activity of DOT cells in human patients. For
instance, which concentration of these cytokines is required for the activity/support of
these cells in vitro, and how does that correlate with expected levels in relevant tissues
in a CMV-infected SOTR patient receiving the DOT therapy?
Reply: In our hands, the optimal concentration of IL-15 required to support DOT cell
proliferation in vitro is 70 ng/mL, while the concentration of IL-18 needed in vitro to
potentiate anti-CMV activity is 50 ng/mL. To the best of our knowledge, cytokine levels
(including IL-18 and IL-15) have never been measured directly in CMV-infected human
tissues. However, serum concentrations of IL-18 increase during CMV infection, reaching
median levels of 2000 pg/mL (PMID: 34216086, reference previously included in the
Discussion, line 375). Taken together, while systemic IL-18 levels in patients are expected
to be lower than the concentrations used in our in vitro assays, local microenvironments
(tissue niches, infected organs) may achieve higher, functionally relevant cytokine
concentrations.
• Figure R3 and main figure 3B: We do not fully agree with the author’s interpretation of
these results. Although from later experiments using functionally knocked-out γδTCR
cells, it can be concluded that DOT cells can recognize CMV-infection in the absence of
γδTCR, the data presented in R3 and 3B are not contributing to this finding. Specifically,
in R3, the authors show the inhibitory eDect of the Vδ1 antibody, which is reducing IFNγ
induction by approximately 50% (and sometimes less). We appreciate the significant
reduction compared to iso control, but the blocking eDect seems incomplete, and
residual δ1 signaling eDects cannot be excluded. Combined with the data presented in
figure 3B, where we see variability of DOT cell response to CMV infection in combination
with Vδ1 blocking antibody on the individual donor level, with most donors showing a
decrease in IFNγ secretion after Vδ1 blocking, and 2 donors showing an opposite eDect.
Grouped together, these changes are not deemed statistically significant diDerent
(P=0,051), however in the context of incomplete Vδ1 blocking and the large variability
observed, the validity of this conclusion can be debated (i.e. the lack of diDerence may
be because residual δ1 signaling is suDicient to maintain a certain level of IFNγ
secretion)
Reply: We agree that in Figure R3 (now Supplementary Figure 5A of the revised
manuscript) the blocking eDect is incomplete. As the reviewers point out, residual Vδ1
TCR signaling could result from this incomplete blocking. We have therefore modified our
interpretation of these results and conclusions as follows (in the Results section, line
182): « In contrast to these observations, adding a Vδ1 TCR blocking antibody to
cocultures did not impact IFNg secretion by DOT cells in response to CMV, as shown for
eight independent donors in Fig. 3b. However, as this result could have been explained
by an incomplete Vδ1 TCR blocking (see Figure. S5a), we undertook to knock out the
gdTCR of DOT cells obtained from three independent donors”.
• Figure 3H: This result raises an interesting observation that merits a brief discussion,
even if speculative – now that the CMV status of the donor cells from which the DOTs are
expanded is made visible, it seems that a trend exists of higher IFNγ induction in CMV +
IL-18 cocultured DOTs from CMV negative donors (ie: gray dots are predominantly in the
upper values, while the red dots dominate the lower values). Do the authors wish to
comment on this interesting trend?
Reply: A trend is indeed visible in Fig. 3h. This trend is visible in the absence of any
blocking, and remains consistent throughout blocking conditions. However in Fig. 2c, the
impact of the DOT cell donor CMV serotype on CMV-induced IFNg secretion was
specifically addressed in a larger cohort of donors (n=13 CMVneg and n=14 CMVpos).
This comparison showed no significant diDerence in between CMVneg and CMVpos
donors.
• Figure 3G: We appreciate the added clarity of activating and blocking antibodies to
entire figure 3. Specifically in figure 3G, the activating label underneath ICAM-1 is
missing. Please add the missing label for additional clarity.
Reply: We have clarified Fig. 3g to indicate that DOT cells were stimulated with
recombinant human ICAM-1, indeed activating LFA-1 on DOT cells. This was also
clarified in the Results section (lines 215-216).
• Lastly, we encountered these 2 minor points:
1. the HSCTR acronym is explained in line 49, but used earlier without an explanation in
line 31 and 33.
Reply: We have now defined the acronym HSCTR when first used in the revised
manuscript (line 31).
2. We noticed that in the abstract and other places in the main text, ‘amplified’ is
changed to ‘expanded’, which fits better in the context of proliferating cells. The authors
should consider making this same change to line 65 and 117, where ‘amplified’ is still
used.
Reply: We have now systematically replaced ‘amplified’ by ‘expanded’ when describing
DOT cells in the revised manuscript.
We consider these points to be addressable, and we look forward to seeing them
incorporated in the final version.
Once again, we thank the authors for their work and responsiveness throughout the
review process.
